chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Al-Hasan ibn Ali who said, 'I heard Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) say: Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon them both) said:'

'When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out, “Where are the patient ones?” So a group of people will stand up. Then a caller will call out, “Where are those who exercised self-control?” So a group of people will stand up.” I said, “May I be your ransom, who are the patient ones?” He said, “The patient ones are those who are patient in performing the obligatory duties, and those who exercise self-control are those who abandon sins.”'

key_terms.الصَّابِرُونَ: The patient ones, those who persevere in obligatory duties
key_terms.الْمُتَصَبِّرُونَ: Those who exercise self-control, specifically in abstaining from sins
key_terms.جَعَلْتُ فَدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a phrase of respect and devotion)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between being patient in worship and exercising self-control from sin according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the distinction is drawn between passive endurance and active spiritual vigilance, where 'Sabirun' are those steadfast in performing obligatory duties (Fara'id) and 'Mutassabirun' are those actively restraining themselves from sins. This classification underscores the Shia emphasis on a balanced piety that combines ritual compliance with moral discipline, a concept central to the works of al-Ahwazi in *Kitab al-Zuhd*. The hadith serves as a practical guide for believers to evaluate their spiritual state on the Day of Judgment based on these two pillars of devotion.
